plates.title: The funnel of witnesses
plates.prompt: An illuminated manuscript page on aged parchment, sepia ink with muted gold leaf accents, divided into nine small roundel scenes connected top to bottom by a single flowing ribbon-line, no lettering anywhere except the short capitalised titles beneath each roundel. At the top: a rain-soaked Milan street where a crowd looks up at a reddish-yellow fireball drifting past a second-floor window before exploding against a church tower's cross (BALL OVER MILAN). The ribbon descends to a scholar bent over trays of old photographic plates searching for a trace of a ball (SEARCHING SKY PLATES). Below, the ribbon forks into two bordered enclosures side by side, each drawn like a framed page-within-a-page: the left enclosure, headed by a gentleman at his study window watching a motionless fireball just outside the glass (BALL AT THE WINDOW), continues downward inside the same frame to a falling sphere bursting into a dozen smaller glowing spheres over a street (BALL BREAKS APART). The right enclosure, headed by a woodshed scene with a startled assistant and a ball drifting through the room (BALL IN THE WOODSHED), continues inside the same frame to a man in bed watching a small orange sphere hover near the window (SPHERE BY THE BED). Both enclosures' ribbons rejoin below into a single scholar's table bearing a ruler and spheres of wildly different sizes, from tiny bead to huge orb (SIZES FROM 1.5 CM TO 15 M). The ribbon continues down to a scene of a scientist struck down by lightning at his apparatus, a false engraving of a ball glowing behind him (RICHMANN'S FATAL SPARK), and finally ends at the bottom in a broken armillary sphere with its pieces scattered, a hand reaching to gather them (GATHERING FRAGMENTED SCIENCE). Palette: warm sepia line work, faded ochre and dull gold leaf, aged cream parchment ground, fine hatching shadows, manuscript-vine borders framing each roundel, generous use of the page's width so the two side-by-side enclosures sit clearly apart before rejoining.

plates.title: Six benchmark cases
plates.prompt: An illuminated manuscript page on aged parchment, sepia ink with muted gold leaf, five small roundel scenes arranged with four in an upper row converging downward into a single scene below, linked by flowing ribbon-lines, no lettering anywhere except the short capitalised titles beneath each roundel. At the top, framed exactly as on the overview page: a scientist struck down by an ordinary lightning bolt at his apparatus while a popular engraving behind him wrongly shows a glowing ball (RICHMANN'S FATAL SPARK), opening this set of landmark cases. Beside and below it, three more scenes stand side by side across the width of the page: a man walking a country road in a thunderstorm as a whirling, barrel-shaped fireball trailing smoke appears ahead of him (FIREBALL ON THE ROAD); a red-hot ball falling from a stormy sky onto a house roof, severing telephone wires before plunging into a water tub beneath a window (BALL INTO THE TUB); and a fenced test range where a rocket-triggered lightning bolt strikes a steel plate, forming a glowing ball of light as distant researchers with cameras look on (TRIGGERED LIGHTNING TEST). Ribbon-lines from all four upper scenes converge downward to a single final roundel at the bottom of the page: three relics displayed together on a shelf like altar offerings — a metal tub, a pane of glass, and a thin spectrogram strip (THREE BENCHMARK RELICS). Palette: warm sepia linework, faded ochre and dull gold leaf highlights, aged cream parchment, fine cross-hatched shadows, manuscript-vine borders framing each roundel, scenes large and clear, spaced across the full width of the page with the four upper scenes visibly converging into the one below rather than crowding a narrow column.

questions.question: According to the article, what does the term "ball lightning" refer to?
questions.referenceAnswer: It refers to a still unexplained group of brief, glowing phenomena in atmospheric electricity that appear seemingly at random, last only a few seconds, and then vanish, sometimes leaving traces.

evidence.quote: the term ball lightning (Kugelblitz, foudre globulaire) stands for a still unexplained group of metastable luminous phenomena in atmospheric electricity

questions.question: Why does the article say most collected material on ball lightning remains anecdotal?
questions.premise: Ball lightning appears seemingly at random and disappears within seconds.
questions.referenceAnswer: Because its unpredictable occurrence in time and place means it is almost never captured by instruments, so nearly all evidence comes from eyewitness accounts rather than recordings.

evidence.quote: Because of its unpredictable occurrence, most of the collected material remains anecdotal.

questions.question: Why did the author choose to focus this review specifically on reports from scientists and trained professionals rather than the general public?
questions.premise: Because sightings are unpredictable and rarely instrumented, most evidence is anecdotal eyewitness testimony.
questions.referenceAnswer: Because direct instrumental monitoring of ball lightning is extremely rare, and even large existing eyewitness databases like Rayle's and McNally's did not record observers' professions or training, so the author sought more credible, detailed testimony from trained observers.

evidence.quote: large databanks like Rayle’s (1966; N = 112 reports) and McNally’s (1966; N = 513 reports) from the US did not ask for observer’s professions and degrees

questions.question: What did lightning researchers Rakov and Uman conclude about the many theories devised to explain ball lightning?
questions.referenceAnswer: They concluded that although many theories had been proposed, none was completely satisfactory, and there might even be more than one type of ball lightning or mechanism producing it.

evidence.quote: There have been many theories devised to explain ball lightning. None is completely satisfactory

questions.question: What problem did the author find with some widely repeated reports attributed to famous scientists, such as Niels Bohr's alleged sighting?
questions.premise: The author focused on reports specifically credited to scientists and trained professionals.
questions.referenceAnswer: Such accounts were often secondhand or lacked supporting detail; for example, the Bohr story came only from someone who said he heard it from Victor Weisskopf, and Martin Ryle's report was quoted without any details.

evidence.quote: Several alleged observations (e.g. of Niels Bohr and Victor Weisskopf), often quoted in science or popular journals, were incorrect or lacked data: Tuck (1971) only wrote that he heard from Weisskopf that Bohr had once seen ball lightning.

questions.question: What did geologist Wilhelm von Haidinger do with his 1868 ball lightning sighting that helped make it a precise scientific record?
questions.referenceAnswer: He carefully measured and sketched the glowing object, determining its angular diameter as 0.83°, and formally reported the observation to the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna.

evidence.quote: Haidinger (see his sketch in Fig. 1) determined the object’s angular diameter as 0.83°.

questions.question: What was paradoxical about physics professor Walther Gerlach's 1927 calculation of the speed of the ball lightning he observed?
questions.referenceAnswer: He calculated the object traveled at about 1225 m/s, roughly Mach 3.6, yet it was described as moving completely silently, with no sonic boom or other acoustic effect that such a speed should produce.

evidence.quote: His speed calculation of 1225 m s−1 is quite amazing, because it means the object travelled at a speed of Mach 3.6 “soundless”, without an acoustic effect (sonic boom).

questions.question: What physical evidence did atmospheric chemist Dmitriev collect after his 1965 ball lightning sighting near the Onega river?
questions.referenceAnswer: He took air samples from the smoke trail left by the object, which showed ozone and nitrogen dioxide concentrations 50 to 100 times higher than normal air.

evidence.quote: The samples contained a maximum of 1.3 mg m−3 ozone (O₃) and 1.6 mg m−3 nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), which was 50–100 times higher than in normal air

questions.question: What physical evidence did Axel Wittmann find after his 1951 childhood sighting that let him later calculate the energy involved?
questions.referenceAnswer: He found circular patches of melted asphalt on the road matching the size of the smaller spheres he had seen, and from the melting point of the asphalt and a water layer he calculated the plasma spheres' energy density at at least 1.9 × 10⁷ J per cubic metre.

evidence.quote: circular patches of melted asphalt on the wet . . . roadway which showed . . . interference colours.
calculated the energy density of the plasma spheres to be at least 1.9 × 10⁷ J m−3

questions.question: Why does the author include childhood ball lightning sightings that were only later recalled by people who became scientists?
questions.premise: Wittmann, who later became an astrophysicist, used his childhood sighting to calculate the plasma spheres' energy density.
questions.referenceAnswer: Although children generally observe things similarly to adults, the author argues their later scientific training may improve the quality and detail of their recalled eyewitness testimony.

evidence.quote: It can be argued that all children have similar observation capabilities. However, scientific training and profession might improve the quality of their recalled eyewitness testimony.

questions.question: Why were weather observers stationed at mountain observatories considered valuable sources of ball lightning reports?
questions.referenceAnswer: They were trained professionals specifically positioned and skilled at noticing and documenting transient weather phenomena, making them well placed to observe and record something as rare as ball lightning.

evidence.quote: Weather observers of meteorological stations are trained and predestined to see and report transient weather phenomena.

questions.question: What concern does the author raise about the growing trend of automating weather stations instead of staffing them with observers?
questions.premise: Weather observers at mountain stations are trained to notice and document rare atmospheric events like ball lightning.
questions.referenceAnswer: He worries that removing trained human observers eliminates high-quality observations of rare phenomena like ball lightning, and it is unclear whether citizen science and mobile phone or webcam footage will make up for this loss.

evidence.quote: The tendency of weather services to do without observers and automate synoptic stations (including German mountaintop observatories) may be justified from an economic standpoint, but it eliminates high-quality observations of rare phenomena such as ball lightning.

questions.question: In the statistical synthesis of the 41 cases, what proportion occurred during an actual thunderstorm versus having no thunderstorm connection at all?
questions.referenceAnswer: About 73% occurred during an actual thunderstorm, 10% shortly before or after one, and 17% had no connection to a thunderstorm.

evidence.quote: 73 % occurred within thunderstorms, 10 % before or after, and 17 % without a connection.

questions.question: What ranges of reported object size and observation duration did the synopsis find among the scientists' and trained observers' cases?
questions.referenceAnswer: Reported sizes ranged from 1.5 cm to 15 m, mostly under 20 cm with several over 1 m, while observation durations ranged from 1.5 to 180 seconds, mostly under 3 seconds.

questions.question: What conclusion does the author draw about trying to define a single "ball lightning norm" given this wide variability among cases?
questions.premise: Reported sizes and durations varied hugely, from under 20 cm to 15 m and from under 3 seconds to 180 seconds.
questions.referenceAnswer: He argues it would be epistemologically odd to define one ball lightning norm and then exclude cases that don't fit it; instead, all detailed case reports should be documented even if some are hard to fit into one general model.

evidence.quote: Epistemologically, it would be odd to define a “ball lightning norm” and a priori exclude cases that do not meet this definition.

questions.question: Despite the popular image of ball lightning killing physicist Georg Wilhelm Richmann in 1753, what does the article say actually caused his death?
questions.referenceAnswer: An investigation with autopsy results showed it was a conventional lightning strike through a non-grounded conductor, not ball lightning.

evidence.quote: From an investigation protocol with autopsy results (Anonymous, 1755, pp. 64–68), it is obvious that it was a conventional lightning accident caused by a non-grounded conductor.

questions.question: What popular image did the Richmann case nonetheless help create for ball lightning?
questions.premise: Richmann's death was actually caused by an ordinary lightning strike through an ungrounded conductor, not true ball lightning.
questions.referenceAnswer: It helped create a deadly, destructive popular image of ball lightning, reinforced by injuries and damage actually caused by ordinary cloud-to-ground lightning strokes.

evidence.quote: Ball lightning acquired a deadly and destructive popular image fed by injuries and damage caused by ordinary cloud–ground strokes.

questions.question: What did the 2012 Qinghai Plateau recording, made with slitless spectroscopy, reveal about the ball lightning's composition?
questions.referenceAnswer: The spectrum showed lines from iron, calcium, silicon, nitrogen, and oxygen, which matched a theory that ball lightning forms when lightning vaporizes soil.

evidence.quote: The ball lightning spectrum showed lines due to Fe, CA, Si, N, and O consistent with the Abrahamson and Dinniss (2002) soil strike theory.

questions.question: How did researchers determine the position, height, and speed of the ball lightning observed at Mitino, Moscow, in 2015?
questions.referenceAnswer: Three independent observers filmed the object with mobile phones from different spots at the same time, and triangulating these simultaneous recordings let researchers work out its position, height above ground (30 to 140 metres), and speed.

evidence.quote: Triangulation of the simultaneous records helped to ascertain position and height above ground, which was between 30 and 140 m.

questions.question: What does the author recommend to help move ball lightning research beyond its current fragmented, individualized state?
questions.premise: Cases like the Qinghai spectroscopy recording and the Mitino video triangulation provide physical, instrument-based evidence beyond ordinary eyewitness testimony.
questions.referenceAnswer: He recommends better coordinating research efforts, using physical-evidence benchmark cases together with digital recordings from widespread mobile phones and webcams to build a systematic, multidisciplinary database against which theories and lab simulations can be tested.

evidence.quote: With physical evidence cases like the Dorstone tub, the Poughquag glass, or the Qinghai spectrum as benchmarks and digital material from abundantly present mobile phones and webcams, systematic multidisciplinary case documentation and discussion can lead to a database against which ball lightning theories and simulations can be critically assessed.

ideas.name: Fear of reputational risk suppresses expert reporting
ideas.statement: Credentialed people who witness something that sounds implausible tend not to publish it, because going on the record risks their professional standing, so the visible published record understates how often experts actually see such things.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without this, the article's repeated complaint about secondhand, undocumented anecdotes involving famous scientists, and its closing appeal for silent witnesses to come forward, would make no sense as a pattern rather than isolated gaps.

occurrences.quote: Several alleged observations (e.g. of Niels Bohr and Victor Weisskopf), often quoted in science or popular journals, were incorrect or lacked data: Tuck (1971) only wrote that he heard from Weisskopf that Bohr had once seen ball lightning.
occurrences.reasoning: Explains why a famous physicist's sighting exists only as secondhand hearsay rather than a direct published account.

occurrences.quote: Published ball lightning reports of scientists are scattered, and even more remain unpublished.
occurrences.reasoning: Asserts that unpublished scientist reports outnumber published ones, which implies a systematic reason experts keep quiet rather than mere chance.

occurrences.quote: Scientists who read the article and who have not reported their experience are invited to share it with the author.
occurrences.reasoning: The direct appeal for silent witnesses only makes sense if some barrier, such as reluctance to go public, is assumed to be keeping them from reporting already.

ideas.name: Independent witnesses agreeing certifies an event really happened
ideas.statement: When several people who could not have coordinated describe the same brief event at the same time and place, their agreement is taken as evidence that something objective occurred, rather than that each one separately imagined it.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Many case write-ups rest their credibility entirely on the number and independence of witnesses rather than on any instrument reading, so without this principle those cases would carry no more weight than a single unverifiable story.
ideas.analogy: Like several strangers on different floors independently reporting the same loud bang at the same minute: no one of them proves it happened, but their agreement does.

occurrences.quote: So we get a 1868 multiple object event with sightings from three inner Vienna districts, Landstrasse, Mariahilf, and Neubau, in a triangle 3.4–1.3–3 km apart, with two similar objects (colour, size, rays) and a different one.
occurrences.reasoning: Treats three separately located sightings as jointly establishing a real multi-object event, which only works if independent agreement counts as corroboration.

occurrences.quote: His uncle, industrialist Christian Wilhelm Foerster, wrote a memory log the following day listing all five observers.
occurrences.reasoning: The next-day log of five named witnesses is offered as what makes a childhood memory credible decades later, relying on strength-in-numbers as proof.

occurrences.quote: Triangulation of the simultaneous records helped to ascertain position and height above ground, which was between 30 and 140 m.
occurrences.reasoning: The use of three separate phone videos to triangulate a position assumes that matching independent records is what turns anecdote into measurement.

ideas.name: Leftover physical traces let you reconstruct an unmeasured event
ideas.statement: Even when no instrument recorded an event while it happened, marks it left behind afterward - a melted patch, a damaged fuse, a scorch mark - can be used to calculate quantities like its energy, speed, or path.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Several of the article's most striking numbers (energy density, trajectory, speed) come from after-the-fact calculations on physical residue, which only count as evidence if such reconstructions are trusted to stand in for a direct measurement.
ideas.analogy: Like a crash investigator calculating a car's speed from the length of its skid marks rather than from a speedometer reading.

occurrences.quote: Taking into account water layer and the melting point of B-80 bitumen, Wittmann "calculated the energy density of the plasma spheres to be at least 1.9 × 10⁷ J m−3"
occurrences.reasoning: Derives a physical quantity purely from the melted asphalt left behind, trusting the residue as a stand-in for direct measurement of the object.

occurrences.quote: Gerlach did his calculations: with a speed of sound of 330 m s−1 and observed times of the lightning’s thunder and the explosion, he got a ball lightning trajectory of 1300 + 1150 = 2450 m.
occurrences.reasoning: Infers an unmeasured flight path and speed from timing of sounds and a later-found impact site, not from watching the object directly.

occurrences.quote: With different ball diameters, an assumed amount of four gallons (18 L) of water, and a temperature rise from 10–20 to 60 °C, the calculations found that at least 2 × 10³ J cm−3 would be involved
occurrences.reasoning: Builds a quantitative energy estimate purely from a secondhand newspaper account and the residual effect on a tub of water, treating the trace as sufficient evidence.

ideas.name: Professional training upgrades eyewitness value
ideas.statement: An account of a rare, fleeting natural event becomes more scientifically useful when the person who saw it has professional training that sharpens how carefully they observe and how precisely they describe what happened.

occurrences.quote: it seems promising to evaluate observation reports by scientists and trained professionals
occurrences.reasoning: States outright the premise that justifies restricting the whole compilation to credentialed witnesses.

occurrences.quote: Singer (1971, chap. 5.B.2) and Stenhoff (1999, chap. 10.4) paid special attention to ball lightning reports coming from scientists or trained professionals.
occurrences.reasoning: Cites prior authors acting on the same assumption to justify the method.

occurrences.quote: Weather observers of meteorological stations are trained and predestined to see and report transient weather phenomena.
occurrences.reasoning: Extends the premise to a new category of observer, treating their job training as what makes their sightings worth collecting.

ideas.name: Ball lightning could be several different phenomena
ideas.statement: The reports gathered under one label may not describe a single physical process; they could be several distinct mechanisms that happen to look similar from the outside.

occurrences.quote: There may be more than one type of ball lightning and more than one mechanism by which ball lightning is generated
occurrences.reasoning: States the hypothesis directly as a conclusion drawn from the scattered, inconsistent case evidence.

occurrences.quote: This has led some researchers (as Rakov and Uman, 2003) to assume several types of ball lightning.
occurrences.reasoning: Explains why the wide variety of outlier cases in the synopsis is treated as expected rather than as a reason to doubt the cases.

occurrences.quote: Uman and colleagues call what was produced not ball lightning but point to interesting effects of different materials under the influence of lightning.
occurrences.reasoning: Shows researchers actively distinguishing a lab-made glowing effect from the natural phenomenon, which only makes sense if 'ball lightning' is not assumed to be one single thing automatically matched by any similar-looking glow.

ideas.name: A field can stay fragmented without one unifying theory
ideas.statement: A research area can accumulate thousands of observations and many competing explanations yet never settle into a single accepted theory, because no decisive test exists to choose among the explanations.

ideas.name: Lightning-location networks can verify anecdotal sightings
ideas.statement: Automated networks that log the time, position, and electrical current of every lightning strike can be checked against a witness's reported time and place, turning an otherwise unverifiable story into a dated, located event with measurable associated current.

quotes.reason: States the central puzzle the whole article addresses: abundant testimony, almost no hard evidence.

quotes.text: They counted almost 5000 observation reports. “There may be more than one type of ball lightning and more than one mechanism by which ball lightning is generated”, they continue, also “There have been many theories devised to explain ball lightning. None is completely satisfactory” and “many luminous phenomena created in the laboratory are claimed by their creators to be ball lightning”.
quotes.reason: Summarizes the unresolved scientific status that motivates collecting expert testimony.

quotes.text: For the same reason, Turner called ball lightning research a “fragmented science” (2001).
quotes.reason: A memorable label for the field's disorganized state, echoed again in the conclusion.

quotes.text: Chances to monitor the transient phenomenon directly are minimal: Tompkins et al. (1975) searched about 12 000 photographic records of the US Prairie Meteorite Network that observed the night sky daily for over 10 years and found two probable ball lightning events.
quotes.reason: Concrete illustration of why direct instrumental evidence is so rare, justifying the eyewitness-based methodology.

quotes.text: Therefore, Singer (1971, chap. 5.B.2) and Stenhoff (1999, chap. 10.4) paid special attention to ball lightning reports coming from scientists or trained professionals. However, large databanks like Rayle’s (1966; N = 112 reports) and McNally’s (1966; N = 513 reports) from the US did not ask for observer’s professions and degrees.
quotes.reason: Explains the gap in existing databases that this article's compilation is designed to fill.

quotes.text: So it seemed to be the right place for an updated case review encompassing published (e.g. Singer, 1971; Stenhoff, 1999) as well as unpublished reports. An international attempt to collect scientists’ reports was beyond the scope of this review, so it does not claim to be complete but can and will be expanded by forthcoming reports in the future.
quotes.reason: States the article's own scope and honest limitation as a growing, non-exhaustive database.

quotes.text: The unexpectedly high number of positive strokes and the equal frequency of close and distant events were discussed at the 34th International Conference on Lightning Protection.
quotes.reason: Highlights a genuinely surprising empirical finding from the author's lightning-correlation study.

quotes.text: His speed calculation of 1225 m s−1 is quite amazing, because it means the object travelled at a speed of Mach 3.6 “soundless”, without an acoustic effect (sonic boom).
quotes.reason: A striking anomaly within one of the most scientifically rigorous case accounts, pointing to an unexplained physical puzzle.

quotes.text: This is one of the rare occasions where ball lightning met a gifted experimental physicist. Gerlach is renowned for his 1922 experiment about spin quantization in a magnetic field.
quotes.reason: Signals why the Gerlach case carries unusual scientific weight among the compiled reports.

quotes.text: A special category of reports is ball lightning encountered by children who, in their later life, followed a scientific career and then described in detail what they saw. It can be argued that all children have similar observation capabilities. However, scientific training and profession might improve the quality of their recalled eyewitness testimony.
quotes.reason: Introduces and justifies a distinct, noteworthy subcategory of evidence within the compilation.

quotes.text: The tendency of weather services to do without observers and automate synoptic stations (including German mountaintop observatories) may be justified from an economic standpoint, but it eliminates high-quality observations of rare phenomena such as ball lightning. Whether this will be compensated by citizen science and the spread of mobile phone and web cameras remains uncertain.
quotes.reason: A forward-looking concern about how automation is eroding a key source of credible evidence.

quotes.text: Thus, even this relatively small sample of educated and trained observers shows a variety of situations, object sizes, and case durations, and some outliers are hard to integrate into one general ball lightning model. This has led some researchers (as Rakov and Uman, 2003) to assume several types of ball lightning.
quotes.reason: Key synthesis point: the diversity of cases resists a single unifying explanation.

quotes.text: Epistemologically, it would be odd to define a “ball lightning norm” and a priori exclude cases that do not meet this definition. Regardless of all problems with an explanatory theory, detailed case reports should be documented.
quotes.reason: States the author's methodological stance against cherry-picking which reports count as 'real' ball lightning.

quotes.text: Ball lightning acquired a deadly and destructive popular image fed by injuries and damage caused by ordinary cloud–ground strokes.
quotes.reason: Explains how a famous but misattributed death (Richmann's) shaped lasting public mythology around ball lightning.

quotes.text: Charcot’s discrimination between keraunoparalysis and neuropsychological aftereffects is still made in medicine (Andrews et al., 2017).
quotes.reason: Notes a lasting medical legacy from one of the historical ball lightning cases.

quotes.text: This is the whole available case documentation, but the chance to compute the ball’s energy density electrified researchers (Singer, 1971; Stenhoff, 1999).
quotes.reason: Wry observation that a thin, single-source anecdote nonetheless became a major touchstone for quantitative theorizing.

quotes.text: Uman and colleagues call what was produced not ball lightning but point to interesting effects of different materials under the influence of lightning.
quotes.reason: An important caveat distinguishing a rigorous experimental result from an actual ball lightning observation.

quotes.text: The main difference between modern science and Frankenstein’s laboratory is guiding research paradigms that – in the case of natural phenomena – condition a proper order of systematic data acquisition, formation, and testing of hypotheses and theories, and – if possible – laboratory simulation. In the case of ball lightning, the research logic is distorted by a random phenomenon that is hard to observe, irreproducible, and mostly reported by change.
quotes.reason: The article's clearest statement of why ball lightning research defies normal scientific method.

quotes.text: Most ball lightning research was (and still is) part-time and individualized – some people collecting data, some theorizing, some doing laboratory tests. Big databases (e.g. Brand, Stakhanov, Rayle, McNally) ended and amateurs took over, theorists opened at least 16 explanatory domains (Rakov and Uman, 2003, p. 664), and a diversity of laboratory simulations developed laterally.
quotes.reason: Summarizes the fragmented, uncoordinated state of the entire field the article aims to improve.

quotes.text: Nevertheless, the author is still optimistic that scientific progress will be faster when capacities are better coordinated.
quotes.reason: The article's closing thesis and call to action.

quotes.text: With physical evidence cases like the Dorstone tub, the Poughquag glass, or the Qinghai spectrum as benchmarks and digital material from abundantly present mobile phones and webcams, systematic multidisciplinary case documentation and discussion can lead to a database against which ball lightning theories and simulations can be critically assessed.
quotes.reason: States the concrete path forward the article proposes for finally testing ball lightning theories.

entries.name: Ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A short-lived glowing sphere reported during thunderstorms, distinct from ordinary lightning bolts, whose physical cause remains unexplained despite thousands of eyewitness accounts.
entries.background: The term was coined by the French scientist François Arago in his 1837 work on thunder, and has since produced numerous rival theories without a confirmed explanation.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: A 19th-century French astronomer and physicist who wrote an early influential treatise on thunder and lightning, in which he gave the phenomenon its name.

entries.name: Rakov and Uman
entries.background: Vladimir Rakov and Martin Uman co-authored a major reference handbook on all aspects of lightning physics, in which a single chapter reviews the uncertain status of ball lightning research.

entries.name: COST Action
entries.senseHere: A European-funded collaborative research program, here one coordinating physicists studying lightning, whose participants agreed that ball lightning is a real phenomenon.

entries.name: fragmented science
entries.senseHere: A field of study scattered across isolated individual efforts and competing theories, lacking the coordinated structure of mainstream scientific research.
entries.background: This phrase was used by researcher Turner in 2001 to describe the disorganized, piecemeal state of ball lightning research across many independent investigators.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.senseHere: The Austrian network of ground sensors that detects and records the location, timing, and electrical strength of lightning strikes across the country.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.senseHere: A German lightning-detection network that records the position and electrical characteristics of lightning strokes, used here to correlate strikes with reported ball lightning sightings.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: An Austrian geologist and mineralogist and member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Vienna, who recorded one of the earliest detailed scientific ball lightning observations in 1868.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: A German physics professor known for the 1922 Stern-Gerlach experiment on magnetic spin, who later gave a detailed 1927 account of a ball lightning sighting with calculated trajectory and speed.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: A British radio astronomer who later became a professor of physical electronics, whose detailed 1963 airplane sighting of ball lightning was published in Nature and widely cited afterward.

entries.name: Pikes Peak
entries.background: A 4,302-metre mountain in Colorado's Front Range that hosted a Harvard weather observatory in the late 19th century, where staff recorded early ball lightning incidents during lightning strikes.

entries.name: Puy de Dôme
entries.background: A 1,465-metre extinct volcano in France's Massif Central that holds a long-running weather and physics observatory, site of a 1916 multi-event ball lightning report by its staff.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: A Baltic German physicist and member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences who was killed in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity, an accident later mythologized in popular depictions as a ball lightning strike.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: A temporary paralysis or numbness in a limb that follows close exposure to lightning or a ball lightning encounter, without lasting physical injury.
entries.background: The neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot used this term to distinguish short-lived nerve effects of a lightning-related shock from longer-lasting psychological trauma in the same patient.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: A pioneering French physician and founder of modern neurology at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris, who taught Sigmund Freud and studied a patient's ball lightning encounter as a case of nerve trauma.

entries.name: triggered lightning
entries.senseHere: Lightning deliberately induced by launching a small rocket trailing a grounded wire into a thundercloud, allowing researchers to study strikes under controlled conditions.
entries.background: Martin Uman's research group used this rocket-and-wire technique at a Florida test site to direct real lightning strikes onto various ground materials and observe the resulting effects.

entries.name: Abrahamson and Dinniss soil strike theory
entries.senseHere: A proposed explanation that ball lightning forms when a lightning strike vaporizes silicon-rich soil, creating a floating ball of burning silicon particles.
entries.background: This theory, developed by researchers Abrahamson and Dinniss in 2002, is one of several competing physical models for what generates ball lightning.

entries.text: Ball lightning has thousands of witnesses but no settled theory; this review bets that expert testimony can help.
The term and a vast literature already exist, yet decades of review have left the field still fragmented and undocumented.
Given few instrumental records, the chosen fix is to mine credentialed witnesses' own accounts rather than wait for cameras.
With fieldwork methods set, the case-by-case test begins: can professional training yield sharper, more consistent sightings.
Scientist testimony assembled, the net widens to non-scientist professionals to see if their reports echo the same patterns.
With dozens of individual accounts gathered, the question becomes whether any shared pattern emerges across them.
Patterns found but inconclusive, so six landmark cases are added to test whether physical traces can anchor the testimony.
Evidence and traces assembled, the open question becomes whether better coordination could finally unify this scattered field.
The compiled testimony stands as offered, its sources open but its explanation still unresolved.

parts.title: 6 Other influential or notable cases
